claim: Perceptual decisions about sensory input are influenced by fluctuations in ongoing neural activity, most prominently driven by attention and neuromodulator systems.
source: Perceptual decisions about sensory input are influenced by fluctuations in ongoing neural activity, most prominently driven by attention and neuromodulator systems.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the overall findings of the study and references to existing literature.

claim: Both attention and catecholaminergic enhancement improved decision-making at the behavioral and algorithmic level, as reflected in increased perceptual sensitivity and the modulation of the drift rate parameter derived from drift diffusion modeling.
source: Both attention and catecholaminergic enhancement improved decision-making at the behavioral and algorithmic level, as reflected in increased perceptual sensitivity and the modulation of the drift rate parameter derived from drift diffusion modeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data (d') and computational modeling results (drift rate) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Attention and catecholaminergic enhancement both modulated pre-stimulus cortical excitability, cue- and stimulus-evoked sensory activity, as well as parietal evidence accumulation signals.
source: Univariate analyses of EEG data time-locked to the attentional cue, the target stimulus, and the motor response further revealed that attention and catecholaminergic enhancement both modulated pre-stimulus cortical excitability, cue- and stimulus-evoked sensory activity, as well as parietal evidence accumulation signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG analyses of alpha power, ERPs, and CPP signals presented in the results.

claim: Similar, unique, and interactive effects of attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation were observed on behavioral, algorithmic, and neural markers of the decision-making process.
source: Interestingly, we observed both similar, unique, and interactive effects of attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation on these behavioral, algorithmic, and neural markers of the decision-making process.
evidence: This claim summarizes the pattern of results across multiple analyses showing main effects and interactions.

claim: Ongoing fluctuations in neural activity may underlie behavioral variability in perceptual decisions.
source: Recent laboratory experiments, meticulously controlling for external factors, have shown that ongoing fluctuations in neural activity may underlie such behavioral variability (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Renart and Machens, 2014; Waschke et al., 2021; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Variability in behavioral responses may find its root cause in alterations in sensory processes leading up toward the decision.
source: Variability in behavioral responses, however, may not be exclusively related to alterations in the decision-making process, but in fact may find its root cause in alterations in sensory processes leading up toward the decision (Benwell et al., 2017; Busch et al., 2009; Iemi et al., 2017; Iemi et al., 2022; Samaha et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attention to specific features of sensory input results in facilitated processing of this input and is associated with improved behavioral performance.
source: Attention to specific features of sensory input (e.g. its spatial location or content) results in facilitated processing of this input and is associated with improved behavioral performance (Carrasco, 2011; Desimone and Duncan, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The central arousal state of animals is controlled by the activity of neuromodulators, including noradrenaline and acetylcholine.
source: The central arousal state of animals is controlled by the activity of neuromodulators, including noradrenaline (NA; Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005) and acetylcholine (ACh; Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; McCormick, 1989), which globally innervate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The relation between noradrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulator activity and behavioral performance is non-monotonic, with optimal behavioral performance occurring at intermediate levels of neuromodulation.
source: Contrary to attention, the relation between noradrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulator activity and behavioral performance is non-monotonic, with optimal behavioral performance occurring at intermediate levels of neuromodulation (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bentley et al., 2011; McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both attention and neuromodulators can alter the input/output ratio (or: gain) of single neurons and neuronal networks.
source: Both attention and neuromodulators can alter the input/output ratio (or: gain) of single neurons and neuronal networks, thereby modulating the impact of (sensory) input on cortical processing (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Humphreys et al., 1998; Soma et al., 2012) and thus possibly perceptual experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recordings in macaque middle temporal area have provided evidence for attentional modulation of neural gain, by showing increased firing rates for neurons having their receptive field on an attended location in space, but suppressed firing rates for neurons with receptive fields outside that focus, under identical sensory input.
source: For example, recordings in macaque middle temporal area have provided evidence for attentional modulation of neural gain, by showing increased firing rates for neurons having their receptive field on an attended location in space, but suppressed firing rates for neurons with receptive fields outside that focus, under identical sensory input (Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Both NA and ACh are known to modulate firing rates of neurons in sensory cortices.
source: Likewise, both NA and ACh are known to modulate firing rates of neurons in sensory cortices (McCormick, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The arousal state of mice, driven by neuromodulator activity, strongly modulates ongoing membrane potentials in auditory cortex and can shape optimal states for auditory detection behavior.
source: To illustrate, the arousal state of mice, driven by neuromodulator activity, strongly modulates ongoing membrane potentials in auditory cortex and as such can shape optimal states for auditory detection behavior (McGinley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neuromodulator activity and attention have similar effects on network dynamics, as both increase cortical desynchronization and enhance the encoding of sensory information.
source: Neuromodulator activity and attention also have similar effects on network dynamics, as both increase cortical desynchronization and enhance the encoding of sensory information (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ATX is a relatively selective NA reuptake inhibitor, which inhibits the presynaptic NA reuptake transporter, thereby resulting in increased NA and dopamine levels.
source: ATX is a relatively selective NA reuptake inhibitor, which inhibits the presynaptic NA reuptake transporter, thereby resulting in increased NA and dopamine levels (Simpson and Plosker, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research describing the pharmacological properties of ATX.

claim: DNP is a cholinesterase inhibitor, which impedes the breakdown of ACh by cholinesterase, thereby resulting in overall increased ACh levels.
source: DNP is a cholinesterase inhibitor, which impedes the breakdown of ACh by cholinesterase, thereby resulting in overall increased ACh levels (Tiseo et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research describing the pharmacological properties of DNP.

claim: The robust effects of ATX, but absence of effects under DNP are in line with previous non-clinical reports.
source: The robust effects of ATX, but absence of effects under DNP are in line with previous non-clinical reports (Pfeffer et al., 2018; Pfeffer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Forced-choice guessing at the end of the day about receiving any active substance suggested that some participants may have been aware of being in a drug session.
source: However, forced-choice guessing at the end of the day about receiving any active substance (ATX, DNP) or not (PLC) suggested that some participants may have been aware of being in a drug session (proportion z-tests ATX vs. PLC: z=2.96, p=0.003; DNP vs. PLC: z=0.55, p=0.10).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of forced-choice guessing data.

claim: Validly cued trials were associated with increased drift rates.
source: We indeed found that validly cued trials were associated with increased drift rates. This can be observed in Figure 2D by a clear divergence of the posterior probability distributions for the ATX model (in blue) and the DNP model (in green) from 0 (both models p<0.001; Figure 2D, 'cue validity effects').
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased drift rate was observed under ATX, but not for DNP.
source: We also observed increased drift rate under ATX (in blue), but not for DNP (ATX model: p=0.02, DNP model: p=0.09; Figure 2D, 'drug effects').
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ATX increased the effects of cue validity on drift rate, but the effect size was small in comparison to the main effects of ATX and cue validity.
source: Moreover, ATX increased the effects of cue validity on drift rate, but the effect size was small in comparison to the main effects of ATX and cue validity (ATX model: p=0.02; x̄interaction=0.04; Figure 2D, 'interaction effects').
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Although the rate of evidence accumulation was increased under ATX, the onset of this accumulation was delayed, indexed by an increase in non-decision time.
source: Although the rate of evidence accumulation was increased under ATX, the onset of this accumulation was delayed, indexed by an increase in non-decision time (ATX model: p=0.048, DNP model: p=0.09; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cue validity and drug did not affect decision bound separation, showing that response caution was not under the influence of neuromodulation or attention.
source: Cue validity and drug did not affect decision bound separation, showing that response caution was not under the influence of neuromodulation or attention (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No effects of cue validity or drug on drift rate variability were observed showing that the overall rate, and not the consistency, of evidence accumulation was enhanced by ATX and cue validity.
source: We observed no effects of cue validity or drug on drift rate variability showing that the overall rate, and not the consistency, of evidence accumulation was enhanced by ATX and cue validity (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cued stimuli triggered a more positive (or less negative) ERP response than uncued stimuli already early on, specifically from 70 ms to 336 ms post-stimulus.
source: First, cued stimuli triggered a more positive (or less negative) ERP response than uncued stimuli already early on, specifically from 70 ms to 336 ms post-stimulus (two clusters: 70–125 ms, p=0.043; 141–336 ms, p<0.001; Figure 4C – left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of stimulus-locked ERP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The main effect of stimulus identity on occipito-temporal activity (difference between target vs. noise stimuli) occurred later in time, from 352 ms to 500 ms post-stimulus.
source: Second, the main effect of stimulus identity on occipito-temporal activity (difference between target vs. noise stimuli) occurred later in time, from 352 ms to 500 ms post-stimulus (p=0.01; Figure 4C – middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of stimulus-locked ERP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Drug condition affected ERP amplitudes relatively late in time (406–586 ms).
source: Third, and finally, similar to the effect of stimulus identity, drug condition affected ERP amplitudes relatively late in time (406–586 ms; p=0.004; Figure 4C – right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of stimulus-locked ERP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neural activity for the hemisphere associated with the cued location (contra) was clearly different than for the uncued location (ipsi) in two time-windows (89–175 ms, p=0.002; 198–363 ms, p<0.001).
source: Neural activity for the hemisphere associated with the cued location (contra) was clearly different than for the uncued location (ipsi) in two time-windows (89–175 ms, p=0.002; 198–363 ms, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of cue-locked ERP data.

claim: Attentional cues resulted in a stronger suppression of alpha-band power for the hemisphere associated with the cued location (contra) compared to the uncued (ipsi) location.
source: Replicating previous work, the time-frequency (TF) spectrum plotted in Figure 5C shows that attentional cues resulted in a stronger suppression of alpha-band power for the hemisphere associated with the cued location (contra) compared to the uncued (ipsi) location.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-frequency analyses shown in Figure 5C and citations to previous research.

claim: Stronger alpha-band desynchronization for cued vs uncued locations was observed 120 ms from cue onset until target stimulus onset.
source: Stronger alpha-band desynchronization for cued vs uncued locations was observed 120 ms from cue onset until target stimulus onset (p<0.001; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of alpha power shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a main effect of drug on total alpha power over both the hemisphere associated with the cued location and the hemisphere associated with the uncued location from 659 ms to 1253 ms after cue onset.
source: Moreover, there was a main effect of drug, revealing that total alpha power over both the hemisphere associated with the cued location and the hemisphere associated with the uncued location was modulated by drug from 659 ms to 1253 ms after cue onset (p=0.02; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of alpha power shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ATX reduced overall alpha-band power for both cued (contra) and uncued (ipsi) locations, with respect to PLC, so not in a lateralized manner.
source: This latter result shows that ATX reduced overall alpha-band power for both cued (contra) and uncued (ipsi) locations, with respect to PLC, so not in a lateralized manner.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the statistical results showing main effects but no interactions.

claim: The effect of the spatial cue on prestimulus alpha-band power lateralization in the late time-window was related to the cue effect on perceptual sensitivity and this relation was not different between the drug sessions.
source: The effect of the spatial cue on prestimulus alpha-band power lateralization in this late time-window was related to the cue effect on perceptual sensitivity and this relation was not different between the drug sessions (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1B for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ATX increased the lateralized cue-locked ERP component (EDAN) by enhancing the difference between cued (contra) and uncued (ipsi) locations, suggesting enhanced attentional orientation in a hemisphere-specific manner.
source: Interestingly, ATX increased the lateralized cue-locked ERP component (EDAN) by enhancing the difference between cued (contra) and uncued (ipsi) locations, suggesting enhanced attentional orientation in a hemisphere-specific manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of cue-locked ERP data shown in Figure 5A and represents an interpretation of the results.

claim: Prestimulus occipital alpha power, an index of cortical excitability, was bilaterally decreased under ATX, and did not relate to the attentional cue, suggesting that enhanced catecholaminergic levels regulate cortical excitability in a spatially non-specific and global manner.
source: However, in contrast, prestimulus occipital alpha power, an index of cortical excitability (Capotosto et al., 2009; Händel et al., 2011; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010), was bilaterally decreased under ATX, and did not relate to the attentional cue, suggesting instead that enhanced catecholaminergic levels regulate cortical excitability in a spatially non-specific and global manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of alpha power shown in Figure 5C and represents an interpretation of the results with citations to previous research.

claim: Computational modeling of choice behavior showed that both the allocation of attention to target stimuli and increased catecholaminergic levels enhanced the rate of sensory evidence accumulation (drift rate), resulting in improved perceptual sensitivity.
source: Computational modeling of choice behavior showed that both the allocation of attention to target stimuli (rotated Gabor patches) and increased catecholaminergic levels enhanced the rate of sensory evidence accumulation (drift rate, Figure 2D), resulting in improved perceptual sensitivity (effect was stronger for attention, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figures 2A and 2D.

claim: The effects of attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation on stimulus-locked neural activity over occipito-temporal electrodes occurred at different latencies.
source: First, we observed that the effects of attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation on stimulus-locked (Gabor) neural activity over occipito-temporal electrodes occurred at different latencies. Attention modulated sensory processing much earlier in time (starting ~70 ms after stimulus presentation) than the catecholaminergic intervention (starting ~400 after stimulus presentation; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-corrected statistical analyses of stimulus-locked ERP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both spatial attention and catecholamines modulated alpha-band desynchronization, but attention did so unilaterally, whereas catecholaminergic modulation of alpha-band desynchronization was bilateral.
source: Second, both spatial attention and catecholamines modulated alpha-band desynchronization, a marker of cortical excitability (Figure 5D), but attention did so unilaterally, as reflected in stronger alpha-band desynchronization in the hemisphere opposite to the locus of attention, whereas catecholaminergic modulation of alpha-band desynchronization was bilateral (no hemispherical specificity nor interaction with attentional cue).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of alpha power shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Prestimulus cortical excitability (alpha power) and stimulus-locked activity related to the processing of visual input were differentially modulated by spatial attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation.
source: Thus, prestimulus cortical excitability (alpha power) and stimulus-locked activity related to the processing of visual input were differentially modulated by spatial attention and catecholaminergic neuromodulation.
evidence: This claim is a summary inference drawn from the results on alpha power and stimulus-locked ERPs.

claim: Effects of attention on drift rate were increased under catecholaminergic enhancement.
source: We did observe two striking interaction effects between the catecholaminergic system and spatial attention. First, effects of attention on drift rate were increased under catecholaminergic enhancement (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Although the interaction effect between attention and ATX on drift rate was not reflected in CPP slope/peak amplitude, this suggests that catecholamines and spatial attention might together shape sensory evidence accumulation in a multiplicative manner.
source: Although this interaction effect was not reflected in CPP slope/peak amplitude, this does suggest that catecholamines and spatial attention might together shape sensory evidence accumulation in a multiplicative manner.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference drawn from the drift rate interaction results.

claim: Spatial attention and neuromodulation showed similar, unique, and interactive effects on neural activity underlying different stages of the perceptual decision-making process.
source: Taken together, spatial attention and neuromodulation showed similar, unique, and interactive effects on neural activity underlying different stages of the perceptual decision-making process.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement of the overall findings.

claim: Bauer et al., 2012, showed that the effect of (non-probabilistic) spatial cues on prestimulus alpha power lateralization was increased under a cholinergic agonist (physostigmine) compared to PLC.
source: Previously, Bauer et al., 2012, showed that the effect of (non-probabilistic) spatial cues on prestimulus alpha power lateralization was increased under a cholinergic agonist (physostigmine) compared to PLC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: We did not replicate the finding that cholinergic enhancement increases the effect of spatial cues on prestimulus alpha power lateralization, neither for DNP nor ATX.
source: We did not replicate this finding, neither for DNP (elevating cholinergic levels; Figure 5E) nor ATX (elevating catecholaminergic levels; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of alpha power shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pharmacologically elevating tonic neuromodulator levels may have resulted in changes in phasic neuromodulatory responses as well.
source: As such, pharmacologically elevating tonic neuromodulator levels may have resulted in changes in phasic neuromodulatory responses as well.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference about the potential confound in the experimental manipulation.

claim: Response accuracy and response speed are differentially represented in the CPP, with correct vs. erroneous responses resulting in a higher slope and peak amplitude, whereas fast vs. slow responses are only associated with increased slopes.
source: Here, we demonstrated that response accuracy and response speed are differentially represented in the CPP, with correct vs. erroneous responses resulting in a higher slope and peak amplitude, whereas fast vs. slow responses are only associated with increased slopes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of CPP data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: When we compared subjects with high and low drift rates, we observed that both CPP slope and CPP peak were increased for the high vs. low drift group.
source: Regardless, when we compared subjects with high and low drift rates (Figure 3C), we observed that both CPP slope and CPP peak were increased for the high vs. low drift group (independent of the drug or attentional manipulation).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses of CPP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both CPP slope and CPP peak were associated with drift rate from the DDM.
source: This indicates that both CPP slope and CPP peak were associated with drift rate from the DDM.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the correlation between CPP features and drift rate.

claim: In line with previous non-clinical studies that report physiological responses of 5 mg DNP, we did not observe consistent subjective or physiological effects of DNP.
source: In line with previous non-clinical studies that report physiological responses of 5 mg DNP (Pfeffer et al., 2018; Pfeffer et al., 2021), we did not observe consistent subjective or physiological effects of DNP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the physiological measurements and citations to previous research.

claim: Even in the absence of autonomic markers, 5 mg DNP has been shown to induce behavior and neural activity, related to visual perception.
source: However, even in the absence of such autonomic markers, 5 mg DNP has been shown to induce behavior and neural activity, related to visual perception (Boucart et al., 2015; Gratton et al., 2017; Pfeffer et al., 2018; Pfeffer et al., 2021; Silver et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: DNP and ATX effects were mirrored, with a recent study using DNP and ATX in combination with whole-brain fMRI revealing that these neuromodulator systems have opposite effects on cortex-wide connectivity patterns.
source: Corresponding with our observation that DNP and ATX effects were mirrored, a recent study using DNP and ATX in combination with whole-brain fMRI revealed that these neuromodulator systems have opposite effects on cortex-wide connectivity patterns, even though both systems enhanced neural gain (Pfeffer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and the observed pattern of results in the current study.

claim: Catecholamines enhanced and ACh suppressed cortex-wide auto-correlation of activity, suggested to reflect intracortical signaling by lateral and feedback processes.
source: More specifically, catecholamines enhanced and ACh suppressed cortex-wide auto-correlation of activity (Pfeffer et al., 2021), suggested to reflect intracortical signaling by lateral and feedback processes (Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Silver et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High cholinergic levels are associated with enhanced afferent input to cortex (feedforward) but decreased feedback drive.
source: Furthermore, high cholinergic levels are associated with enhanced afferent input to cortex (feedforward) but decreased feedback drive (Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Both evidence accumulation processes and target selection processes strongly rely on cortical feedback.
source: Because both evidence accumulation processes and target selection processes strongly rely on cortical feedback (Boehler et al., 2009; Dehaene et al., 2011; Donohue et al., 2020; Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Murphy et al., 2021; Pereira et al., 2022; Pitts et al., 2014; Seijdel et al., 2021; Theeuwes, 2010; Wang, 2008), the mirrored (compared to ATX) effects of DNP on the neural markers of these processes may have been caused by interrupted feedback processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a speculative interpretation of the DNP results.

claim: The study was approved by the Medical Ethical Committee of the Amsterdam Medical Centre (AMC) and the local ethics committee of the University of Amsterdam.
source: This study was approved by the Medical Ethical Committee of the Amsterdam Medical Centre (AMC) and the local ethics committee of the University of Amsterdam.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after explanation of the experimental protocol.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after explanation of the experimental protocol.
evidence: This is a statement about the consent procedure.

claim: Two participants decided to withdraw from the experiment after having performed the first experimental session.
source: Two participants decided to withdraw from the experiment after having performed the first experimental session. The data from these participants are not included in this work, resulting in N=28.
evidence: This is a statement about participant attrition.

claim: The half-life of ATX varies between 4.5 and 19 hr and peak plasma levels are reached ~2 hr after administration.
source: The half-life of ATX varies between 4.5 and 19 hr and peak plasma levels are reached ~2 hr after administration.
evidence: This is a statement about the pharmacokinetics of ATX.

claim: The elimination half-life of DNP is 70 hr and peak plasma levels are reached after ~4 hr.
source: The elimination half-life of DNP is 70 hr and peak plasma levels are reached after ~4 hr.
evidence: This is a statement about the pharmacokinetics of DNP.

claim: Minor side-effects were reported by participants, including a mild headache and mild nausea.
source: Minor side-effects were reported by our participants, including a mild headache (1 DNP session, 2 ATX session) and mild nausea (1 DNP session, 4 ATX sessions).
evidence: This is a statement about side effects observed in the study.

claim: Other side-effects, such as fatigue and tenseness, were equally present across all drug sessions including PLC.
source: Other side-effects, such as fatigue and tenseness, were equally present across all drug sessions including PLC.
evidence: This is a statement about side effects observed in the study.
